mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four pillars of OOP?
x: Encapsulation is bundling data with methods and restricting direct access to internal state. It is one of the four pillars, so it does not fit a NOT question.
Inheritance is letting a class reuse and extend another class's members. It is one of the four pillars, so it does not fit a NOT question.
Polymorphism is one interface behaving in different forms depending on the object. It is one of the four pillars, so it does not fit a NOT question.
mcq.e: Compilation is a build step that translates source code into an executable form, not a design pillar. The four pillars are abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.

mcq.q: A blueprint or template from which objects are created is a:
x: The object is an instance created from a class, not the blueprint itself. Objects are the things made from a class template.
A method is a function defined inside a class to perform an action. It is not a template for creating objects.
A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces. It organizes code but does not create objects.
mcq.e: A class is the blueprint that defines the fields and methods an object will have. Objects are created from it, for example with the new keyword in Java.

mcq.q: An instance of a class is called a:
x: An interface is a contract listing method signatures a class must implement. It describes behavior but is not an instance of a class.
A constructor is a special method that initializes a new object. It is used when creating an instance, not the instance itself.
A module is a unit of code organization, such as a file or library. It groups code and is not an instance of a class.
mcq.e: An object is a concrete instance created from a class, holding its own state. Each object has its own values for the fields defined by its class.

mcq.q: Bundling data and methods and hiding internal state is:
x: Abstraction is hiding complexity by exposing only essential features. It is related, but it describes what is exposed rather than bundling data with hidden internal state.
Inheritance is a class reusing and extending another class's members. It concerns sharing code between classes, not bundling and hiding data.
Polymorphism is one interface taking many forms at run time or compile time. It concerns behavior variation, not hiding internal state.
mcq.e: Encapsulation groups data and the methods that operate on it in one class, and restricts direct access to the internal state. Private fields with public methods are a common example.

mcq.q: Exposing only essential features while hiding implementation details is:
x: Encapsulation is bundling data with methods and restricting direct access to internal state. It hides details, but its focus is protecting state rather than exposing essential features.
Overloading is defining methods with the same name but different parameter lists. It is about method naming, not exposing essential features.
Cohesion is how strongly the responsibilities inside one module are related. It is a design quality measure, not an OOP feature for hiding implementation.
mcq.e: Abstraction shows only the essential features of an object and hides how they are implemented. Interfaces and abstract classes are common ways to express it.

mcq.q: Creating a new class from an existing class to reuse its members is:
x: Polymorphism is one interface or method call behaving differently across objects. It concerns behavior variation, not reusing members from a parent class.
Encapsulation is bundling data with methods and restricting direct access. It concerns protecting state, not creating a class from an existing one.
Instantiation is creating an object from a class. It creates instances, not new classes built from existing ones.
mcq.e: Inheritance lets a subclass take on the fields and methods of a parent class, and extend or override them. It models an is-a relationship.

mcq.q: Private variables with public getters and setters illustrate:
x: Inheritance is a class reusing and extending another class's members. It concerns sharing code between classes, not restricting access to fields.
Polymorphism is one interface taking many forms depending on the object. It concerns method behavior, not controlling access through getters and setters.
Overloading is defining methods with the same name but different parameter lists. It concerns method signatures, not hiding fields behind getters and setters.
mcq.e: Encapsulation keeps fields private and exposes controlled access through getters and setters. This protects the internal state and allows validation when it changes.

mcq.q: Which concept allows the same method call to behave differently depending on the object?
x: Encapsulation is bundling data with methods and hiding internal state. It protects state but does not make one call behave differently across objects.
Composition is building a class from objects of other classes as parts. It is a has-a design choice, not a way for one call to behave differently.
Aggregation is a has-a relationship where parts can exist independently of the whole. It describes ownership, not varying behavior of a method call.
mcq.e: Polymorphism lets one method call produce different behavior depending on the actual object. Overriding and interface implementations are typical examples.

mcq.q: Method overloading is an example of:
x: Run-time polymorphism is method overriding, where the call is resolved while the program runs. Overloading is decided at compile time, so this does not fit.
Inheritance is a class reusing members from a parent class. It is a separate pillar and does not describe choosing among overloaded methods.
Encapsulation is restricting direct access to internal state. It does not describe multiple methods sharing one name.
mcq.e: Method overloading is resolved at compile time, based on the parameter list of the call. The compiler picks the matching version before the program runs.

mcq.q: Method overriding is an example of:
x: Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading, resolved by the compiler from the parameter list. Overriding is resolved at run time, so this does not fit.
Static binding is linking a method call at compile time. Overriding uses dynamic binding, so this is the wrong term.
Abstraction is hiding implementation details and exposing essential features. It is a separate pillar and does not describe a subclass replacing a parent method.
mcq.e: Method overriding lets a subclass provide its own version of an inherited method. Java picks the version by the actual object type while the program runs.

mcq.q: Method overloading requires methods with the same name but different:
x: Return types alone cannot distinguish overloads in Java, since the call would be ambiguous. Overloads must differ in their parameter list.
Access modifiers do not affect overload resolution. Changing only the access level does not create a valid overload.
The class name is the same for all methods in one class, so it cannot distinguish overloads. Methods are told apart by their parameters.
mcq.e: Overloading uses methods with the same name in one class but different parameter lists, such as different numbers or types of parameters. The compiler chooses the match at compile time.

mcq.q: A special method called when an object is created is a:
x: A destructor is a method that cleans up when an object is destroyed. It runs at the end of an object's life, not when it is created.
A getter is a method that returns the value of a field. It reads state and is not called automatically when an object is created.
A static method belongs to the class rather than an object and is called without an instance. It is not automatically run when an object is created.
mcq.e: A constructor is a special method that runs when an object is created, typically to initialize its fields. In Java it has the same name as the class.

mcq.q: Which statement is true about a Java constructor?
mcq.a: It has the same name as the class and no return type
x: A constructor has no return type, so it does not return void. Declaring a return type of void would make it an ordinary method.
Constructors are not inherited by subclasses. A subclass calls its parent's constructor through super instead.
Constructors cannot be final, abstract or static. Declaring one as final is not allowed.
mcq.e: A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type. It runs when an object is created with the new keyword.

mcq.q: In Python, the constructor method is named:
x: __new_obj__ is not a Python special method name. Python uses __new__ to create instances and __init__ to initialize them.
The word constructor is not a Python method name. Python does not use a method named constructor.
__start__ is not a Python special method for object creation. It has no meaning to Python's object model.
mcq.e: In Python, __init__ is the special method that initializes a newly created object. It receives self as its first parameter.

mcq.q: The keyword that refers to the current object in Java is:
x: self is the conventional name for the first parameter of a Python method, not a Java keyword. Java uses this.
super refers to the parent class, not the current object. It is used to call parent constructors or methods.
current is not a Java keyword. Java refers to the current object with this.
mcq.e: The Java keyword this refers to the current object. It is used to access fields or call other constructors of the same class.

mcq.q: The keyword that refers to the parent class in Java is:
x: this refers to the current object, not the parent class. It accesses the object's own members.
parent is not a Java keyword. Java uses super for the parent class.
base is the keyword for the parent class in C#, not Java. Java uses super.
mcq.e: The Java keyword super refers to the parent class. It is used to call the parent's constructor or an overridden method.

mcq.q: In Python, the first parameter of an instance method that refers to the object is conventionally:
x: this is the Java and C++ keyword for the current object, not the Python convention. Python methods name the first parameter self.
me is legal as a parameter name in Python, but it is not the convention. Python style uses self.
obj is a generic variable name, not the conventional first parameter name. Python style uses self for the instance.
mcq.e: In Python, the first parameter of an instance method is conventionally named self. It refers to the object the method was called on.

mcq.q: Members declared static belong to:
mcq.a: The class, shared by all objects
x: Each object separately describes instance members, which each object owns. Static members are shared by all objects of the class instead.
Only subclasses is not what static means. Static members belong to the class itself and are accessible regardless of subclassing.
The JVM only is not the meaning of static. The JVM runs bytecode, while static is a language feature of the class.
mcq.e: A static member belongs to the class itself, so one copy is shared by all objects. It can be accessed through the class name without creating an object.

mcq.q: In Java, which keyword prevents a class from being inherited?
x: static means a member belongs to the class rather than an object. It does not stop a class from being extended.
abstract means a class cannot be instantiated and must be subclassed. It requires inheritance, so it does not prevent it.
sealed restricts which classes may extend a class and was finalized in Java 17, not Java 8. It is not a Java 8 keyword.
mcq.e: The final keyword on a class prevents any other class from extending it. For example, the String class in the Java library is declared final.

mcq.q: Which Java keyword is used by a class to inherit another class?
x: implements is used by a class to adopt an interface, not to inherit from another class. Java uses extends for classes.
inherits is not a Java keyword. Java uses extends to declare inheritance.
super refers to the parent class and calls its members. It does not declare the inheritance relationship.
mcq.e: The keyword extends declares that a class inherits from another class. A Java class can extend only one class.

mcq.q: Which Java keyword is used by a class to adopt an interface?
x: extends is used between classes or between interfaces, not for a class adopting an interface. Adopting an interface uses implements.
using is not a Java keyword. Java has no using statement for adopting interfaces.
interface declares a new interface type. It does not state that an existing class adopts one.
mcq.e: The keyword implements is used by a class to adopt an interface and provide bodies for its methods. A class can implement several interfaces.

mcq.q: A class that cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract methods is:
x: A final class cannot be extended. It is the opposite of an abstract class, which must be subclassed.
A static class is a nested class that belongs to an outer class. Top-level Java classes cannot be declared static, and this is not an abstract type.
A wrapper class such as Integer wraps a primitive value in an object. It is not a class that can contain abstract methods.
mcq.e: An abstract class is declared with the abstract keyword and cannot be instantiated directly. It may contain abstract methods that subclasses must implement.

mcq.q: Which can a class implement more than one of in Java?
x: Abstract classes cannot be combined this way, since Java supports only single class inheritance. A class extends only one class.
Final classes cannot be extended at all, so a class cannot extend or implement them. Final is a restriction on inheritance, not a multiple-inheritance mechanism.
Enums are special class types declared with the enum keyword. A class does not implement an enum, and enums cannot be extended.
mcq.e: A Java class can extend only one class but implement many interfaces. Interfaces are how Java gives a class multiple types without multiple class inheritance.

mcq.q: Which access modifier allows access only within the same class?
x: protected allows access from subclasses and the same package, which is wider than the same class. It does not restrict access to the class alone.
public allows access from any class anywhere. It is the widest access level.
default, or package-private, allows access from the same package. It is not limited to the same class.
mcq.e: The private modifier restricts access to members within the same class. Other classes, including subclasses, cannot access them directly.

mcq.q: Which access modifier allows access from subclasses and the same package, but not the world?
x: private restricts access to the same class only. Subclasses in other packages cannot access private members.
public allows access from anywhere, including the world. It is wider than the question allows.
default, or package-private, allows only the same package. It does not give subclasses outside the package access.
mcq.e: The protected modifier allows access from the same package and from subclasses, even those in other packages. It is hidden from the rest of the world.

mcq.q: Multiple inheritance of classes is NOT supported in:
x: C++ supports multiple inheritance of classes, with explicit rules for resolving conflicts. It is not a language that lacks it.
Python supports multiple inheritance of classes, using its method resolution order. It is not a language that lacks it.
Lisp, with CLOS, supports multiple inheritance of classes. It is not a language that lacks it.
mcq.e: Java allows a class to extend only one class, though it can implement multiple interfaces. This avoids the diamond problem but limits class-based reuse.

mcq.q: The ambiguity problem with multiple inheritance is called the:
x: The pigeonhole principle is a combinatorics idea about placing items into boxes. It is a math principle, not an inheritance ambiguity.
The halting problem asks whether a program will finish running and is undecidable. It is a computability question, not an inheritance ambiguity.
The knapsack problem is an optimization problem about packing items under a capacity. It is not an inheritance ambiguity.
mcq.e: The diamond problem occurs when a class inherits from two classes that share a common base, making which inherited method to use ambiguous. C++ and Python handle it differently.

mcq.q: "A Car has an Engine" is an example of:
x: Inheritance is an is-a relationship, such as a Dog being an Animal. Here the Car has a part, so it is not inheritance.
Polymorphism is one interface behaving differently depending on the object. It does not describe one object containing another as a part.
Overloading is defining methods with the same name and different parameters. It does not describe objects containing other objects.
mcq.e: This is a has-a relationship: the Car holds an Engine as a part. It is modeled with a field referencing the Engine object rather than with inheritance.

mcq.q: "A Dog is an Animal" is an example of:
x: Composition is a has-a relationship where one object contains another as a part. A Dog is not a part of an Animal.
Aggregation is a has-a relationship where parts can exist independently. It is not an is-a relationship.
Association is a general link between objects that use each other. It does not express that one class is a kind of another.
mcq.e: This is inheritance, an is-a relationship where the subclass Dog is a more specific kind of the parent class Animal. Dog inherits the members of Animal.

mcq.q: Java source code is compiled to:
x: Machine code for each OS is native code, which Java does not produce directly. Java compiles to bytecode that the JVM translates for each platform.
Assembly is a low-level human-readable form of machine instructions. Java does not compile to assembly.
Source maps map compiled code back to the original source for debugging. They are not the output of compiling Java.
mcq.e: The Java compiler, javac, translates source code into bytecode, a platform-independent instruction format. The JVM then runs that bytecode on each platform.

mcq.q: Bytecode is executed by the:
x: The JDK is the development kit that includes the compiler and tools, and it contains a JVM. It is not the component that executes bytecode alone.
An IDE is an editor or development environment for writing code. It does not execute bytecode.
The JIT compiler is a component inside the JVM that compiles frequently run bytecode to native code. It does not run bytecode as a whole runtime.
mcq.e: The Java Virtual Machine runs bytecode, interpreting it and using a JIT compiler to convert frequently executed code to native machine code. This is what makes Java portable.

mcq.q: "Write Once, Run Anywhere" is associated with:
x: C++ is compiled to native machine code for each platform, so it is not the language behind this slogan. It is not a bytecode language.
Python is an interpreted language and is not the language this bytecode slogan refers to. Its portability comes from its interpreter.
C is compiled to native machine code for each target, so it is not the language behind this slogan. Porting C code needs recompiling.
mcq.e: Write Once, Run Anywhere is Java's slogan, reflecting that compiled bytecode can run on any system with a JVM. It is the core promise of the Java platform.

mcq.q: Which includes the compiler and development tools for Java?
x: The JRE is the runtime environment that runs Java programs, but it lacks the compiler. It is for running programs, not developing them.
The JVM executes bytecode and is not a development kit. It does not include the compiler.
The JIT is a compiler inside the JVM that speeds up execution. It is not the full development kit.
mcq.e: The Java Development Kit, JDK, includes the javac compiler, the JRE and other development tools. It is needed to write and compile Java code.

mcq.q: Who created Java?
x: Bjarne Stroustrup created C++, not Java. Java was developed by James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems.
Guido van Rossum created Python, not Java. He is known as the creator of Python.
Anders Hejlsberg created C# and TypeScript, not Java. He also worked on Turbo Pascal and Delphi.
mcq.e: James Gosling led the team at Sun Microsystems that created Java, released in 1995. He is often called the father of Java.

mcq.q: Who created C++?
x: Dennis Ritchie created the C language, not C++. C++ was created by Bjarne Stroustrup.
James Gosling created Java, not C++. Java was built later and is a different language.
Ken Thompson co-created Unix and the B language, not C++. He did not create C++.
mcq.e: Bjarne Stroustrup created C++ at Bell Labs in the early 1980s as an extension of C with classes. It added object-oriented features to C.

mcq.q: Who created Python?
x: Brendan Eich created JavaScript, not Python. He developed it at Netscape.
Rasmus Lerdorf created PHP, not Python. PHP is mainly a web server language.
Larry Wall created Perl, not Python. Perl is a text-processing language.
mcq.e: Guido van Rossum created Python and released its first version in 1991. He led its development as benevolent dictator for life for many years.

mcq.q: Who created JavaScript at Netscape in 1995?
x: Ryan Dahl created Node.js, which runs JavaScript on servers. He did not create JavaScript itself.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web and HTML. He did not create JavaScript.
Marc Andreessen co-founded Netscape, where JavaScript was developed, but did not create the language.
mcq.e: Brendan Eich developed JavaScript at Netscape in 1995, first under the names Mocha and LiveScript. It was later standardized as ECMAScript.

mcq.q: Who created C#?
x: James Gosling created Java, not C#. Java predates C# and is a different language.
Bjarne Stroustrup created C++, not C#. C# was designed later by Microsoft.
Rasmus Lerdorf created PHP, not C#. PHP is a web scripting language.
mcq.e: Anders Hejlsberg led the design of C# at Microsoft, first released in 2000. He also designed TypeScript and earlier worked on Turbo Pascal and Delphi.

mcq.q: Who created PHP?
x: Larry Wall created Perl, not PHP. Perl is a separate scripting language.
Yukihiro Matsumoto created Ruby, not PHP. Ruby is known for its developer-friendly syntax.
Guido van Rossum created Python, not PHP. Python is a separate general-purpose language.
mcq.e: Rasmus Lerdorf created PHP in the mid-1990s, starting as a set of tools for personal web pages. It later became a widely used server-side language.

mcq.q: The first object-oriented programming language was:
x: Smalltalk is an early object-oriented language from Xerox PARC, developed after Simula. It popularized OOP but was not the first.
C++ was created in the 1980s by Bjarne Stroustrup, long after Simula. It is not the first OOP language.
Java was released in 1995, decades after Simula. It is not the first OOP language.
mcq.e: Simula, developed in Norway in the 1960s, introduced classes, objects and inheritance. It is widely regarded as the first object-oriented programming language.

mcq.q: Which language is credited with popularizing OOP, created by Alan Kay's team at Xerox PARC?
x: Simula, from the 1960s, was the first OOP language, but it was not developed at Xerox PARC. It did not popularize OOP the way Smalltalk did.
Ada is a language designed for the US Department of Defense, not a language from Xerox PARC. Its OOP support came later.
Pascal is a procedural language created by Niklaus Wirth and is not associated with Xerox PARC. It is not an OOP language.
mcq.e: Smalltalk, developed by Alan Kay's team at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, popularized object-oriented programming. It introduced many OOP ideas such as objects that exchange messages.

mcq.q: Which Java block always executes, whether or not an exception occurs?
x: catch handles a specific exception thrown in the try block. It runs only when an exception occurs, not always.
A try block alone does not guarantee that code runs after an exception is thrown. It has no clause that always executes.
throws is a method signature clause declaring exceptions that may be raised. It does not define a block that always runs.
mcq.e: The finally block runs after the try and catch blocks whether or not an exception occurred. This makes it suitable for cleanup such as closing resources.

mcq.q: The Java keyword used to raise an exception is:
x: throws is a method declaration clause listing exceptions a method may raise. It does not raise an exception itself.
raise is not a Java keyword. Python uses raise, while Java uses throw.
catch handles an exception that has been thrown. It does not raise one.
mcq.e: The Java keyword throw raises an exception object at the point where it is used. Execution transfers to the nearest matching catch block.

mcq.q: Which of these is an unchecked exception in Java?
x: IOException is a checked exception that must be caught or declared. It is not a runtime exception.
SQLException is a checked exception for database access errors. It must be handled or declared, so it is not unchecked.
FileNotFoundException is a checked subclass of IOException. It must be handled or declared.
mcq.e: NullPointerException extends RuntimeException, so it is unchecked and need not be declared or caught. It is thrown when code dereferences a null reference.

mcq.q: Java is always:
x: Pass-by-reference means the callee gets the variable itself. Java passes references by value, so this does not describe Java.
Pass-by-name is an old evaluation strategy used in some languages such as Algol. Java does not use it.
Pass-by-pointer is not a Java concept. Java passes references by value and does not expose pointers.
mcq.e: Java is always pass-by-value: method parameters receive a copy of the value, and for objects that copy is of the reference. Reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller.

mcq.q: In Java, == on two object references compares:
x: Contents means the data the objects hold. Comparing contents uses equals(), not the == operator.
Hash codes are integers computed from object contents. The == operator does not compare hash codes.
Types are the classes of the objects. The == operator does not compare types in this way.
mcq.e: For object references, == checks whether both refer to the same object in memory. To compare contents, the equals method is used.

mcq.q: Which method compares the contents of two Java Strings?
x: The == operator compares references, not the characters inside strings. It is the wrong check for contents.
compare() is not a String method in Java. String comparison uses equals() or compareTo().
same() is not a standard String method in Java. It does not exist for content comparison.
mcq.e: The equals() method compares the characters of two String objects and returns true when they match. It is the correct way to test string content.

mcq.q: Strings in Java are:
x: Mutable means the value can change after creation. Java String objects cannot be changed once created.
Primitive is a category for types like int and char. String is an object class, not a primitive.
String is not just a char array. It is a class that provides methods and is immutable, not an array of characters.
mcq.e: Java String objects are immutable, so any change produces a new String rather than modifying the existing one. This makes them safe to share and use as hash keys.

mcq.q: Which Python collection is immutable?
x: list is a mutable sequence whose elements can be changed or added. It does not match an immutable collection.
dict is a mutable mapping of keys to values. It can be changed after it is created.
set is a mutable collection of unique items. Its contents can change, though frozenset is the immutable version.
mcq.e: A tuple is an ordered collection whose elements cannot be changed after creation. It is written with parentheses or commas, such as (1, 2, 3).

mcq.q: In C++, a pure virtual function is declared by appending:
x: = null is not C++ syntax for a pure virtual function. C++ uses = 0 for this.
= void is not valid for declaring a pure virtual function in C++. It does not mark a function as abstract.
= abstract is not C++ syntax. C++ uses the virtual keyword with = 0 and has no abstract keyword.
mcq.e: In C++, appending = 0 to a virtual function declaration makes it pure virtual. A class with at least one pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated.

mcq.q: In C++, the default access in a struct is:
x: private is the default for members of a C++ class, not a struct. A struct's members are public by default.
protected is not the default access level for a struct in C++. It must be stated explicitly.
package is a Java concept with no meaning in C++. C++ has no package access level.
mcq.e: In C++, members of a struct are public by default, while members of a class are private by default. This is the main difference between the two.

mcq.q: In C++, the default access in a class is:
x: public is the default for members of a C++ struct. A class's default is private, so this is not the answer.
protected is not the default access for a class in C++. It must be written explicitly.
internal is a C# access modifier, not a C++ one. C++ has no internal access level.
mcq.e: In C++, members of a class are private by default unless a public or protected label is given. Structs are the variant whose members are public by default.

mcq.q: Which C++ feature lets you use the same operator for user-defined types?
x: Templates let code work with any type through generic programming. They do not define operator behavior for user-defined types.
Friend functions grant a non-member function access to private members. They do not by themselves let an operator be used on user types.
Namespaces group names to avoid conflicts. They do not change how operators behave.
mcq.e: Operator overloading lets a programmer define how operators such as plus or equals work for user-defined types like a Vector or Complex class. It is written as a special operator member or function.

mcq.q: What is the output? Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak(); where Dog overrides speak() to print "Woof"
x: Animal would be the result if the Animal version of speak() ran. Dog overrides speak(), so the overriding version runs at run time.
Compile error is wrong: the reference type Animal declares speak(), so the call is valid and compiles.
Nothing would be printed only if speak() had an empty body. Dog's override prints Woof.
mcq.e: The variable type is Animal but the object is a Dog. Because speak() is overridden, Java uses dynamic dispatch to run Dog's version, which prints Woof.

mcq.q: What does a static counter incremented in the constructor print after three objects are created?
x: 1 would be the count if only one object was created, or if the counter reset each time. Three objects increment it three times.
0 would mean the counter was never incremented, or was a per-object field that resets. It does not match three increments on a shared static counter.
2 is off by one, as if the last object's increment was missed. Each constructor call adds exactly one.
mcq.e: A static field is shared by all objects of the class, so each constructor call increments the same counter. After three objects are created it holds 3.

mcq.q: In Java: try { print A; 5/0; print B } catch(ArithmeticException) { print C } finally { print D }. Output?
x: ABCD would mean B printed after the exception, which cannot happen because 5/0 throws and skips the rest of the try block. The catch block runs next.
AD would mean the catch block was skipped. It does run because ArithmeticException is caught.
ACBD places B after the catch. The statement B is skipped once 5/0 throws, so B never prints.
mcq.e: A is printed, then 5/0 throws ArithmeticException, skipping B. The catch prints C, and finally always prints D, giving ACD.

mcq.q: In Python, what is the output of: class A: __init__ sets x=1; class B(A): __init__ calls super().__init__() then y = x+1; print(B().y)?
x: 1 would result if y were set to x without adding 1. Here y is x plus 1, and x is 1 from A's constructor.
0 would be the value if x were never set or y were not computed correctly. A's constructor sets x to 1.
Error would occur only if super().__init__() were invalid or A had no constructor. In Python 3 the call is valid.
mcq.e: B's constructor calls A's constructor, which sets x to 1. Then y is set to x plus 1, which is 2, so the print statement outputs 2.

mcq.q: Which naming convention uses capital letters for each word including the first, commonly for class names?
x: camelCase starts with a lowercase letter and capitalizes later words. Class names conventionally capitalize the first letter too.
snake_case uses lowercase words joined by underscores. It is used for variables and functions in Python, not class names.
kebab-case joins words with hyphens and is not valid in most identifiers. It is used for URLs and filenames, not class names.
mcq.e: PascalCase capitalizes the first letter of each word, including the first, as in MyClass. It is the usual naming convention for classes in Java and C#.

mcq.q: Which naming convention is typically used for Python variables and functions?
x: PascalCase capitalizes each word and is conventionally used for class names in Python. Functions and variables use snake_case.
SCREAMING_CASE uses uppercase letters with underscores and is used for constants. It is not the convention for ordinary variables or functions.
kebab-case uses hyphens, which are not allowed in Python identifiers. It cannot name a Python variable or function.
mcq.e: snake_case uses lowercase words separated by underscores, such as calculate_total. PEP 8, the Python style guide, recommends it for functions and variables.

mcq.q: Java's automatic memory reclamation is called:
x: Manual deallocation means the programmer frees memory explicitly, as in C. Java frees unused objects automatically instead.
Reference counting only tracks how many references exist to each object. Java's collector is a tracing collector, not reference counting alone.
RAII is a C++ idiom that ties resource release to object lifetime. It is not Java's memory reclamation mechanism.
mcq.e: Garbage collection is Java's automatic memory reclamation, which frees objects that are no longer reachable from the program. The programmer does not free memory explicitly.

mcq.q: Which describes high-quality OO design?
x: Low cohesion and high coupling is the poor design the question describes as undesirable. Modules should be focused and loosely connected.
High coupling and high cohesion mixes a good trait with a bad one. Coupling should be low for good design.
Low cohesion and low coupling makes classes unfocused. Cohesion should be high for good design.
mcq.e: High cohesion means a class has focused, related responsibilities, and low coupling means classes depend on each other minimally. Together they make code easier to change and reuse.

mcq.q: Which Java collection stores unique elements without duplicates?
x: ArrayList is an ordered list that allows duplicate elements. It does not enforce uniqueness.
LinkedList is a list implementation that allows duplicate elements. It does not enforce uniqueness.
Vector is a synchronized dynamic array that allows duplicates. It does not store only unique elements.
mcq.e: HashSet is a Set implementation that stores unique elements with no duplicates, using a hash table internally. Adding an existing element has no effect.

mcq.q: Which Java collection stores key-value pairs?
x: ArrayList stores an ordered sequence of values accessed by index. It holds no keys.
HashSet stores unique values without keys. It is a set, not a map.
Queue stores elements in first-in first-out order. It holds values, not key-value pairs.
mcq.e: HashMap stores key-value pairs and looks up values by their keys. Keys are unique within the map.

mcq.q: JavaScript's strict equality operator is:
x: == is loose equality that converts types before comparing. Strict equality uses === without conversion.
= is the assignment operator, not a comparison. It stores a value in a variable.
!= is loose inequality, which compares with type conversion. It is the negation of ==, not strict equality.
mcq.e: The strict equality operator === returns true only when both operands have the same type and value, with no type conversion. It is recommended for most comparisons.

mcq.q: Which company owns Java today?
x: Sun Microsystems originally developed Java and was acquired by Oracle in 2010. Sun no longer owns Java.
IBM is a separate company that does not own Java. It is known for other software and hardware.
Google is a separate company that developed Android and Dart. It does not own Java.
mcq.e: Oracle acquired Sun Microsystems in 2010, which gave it ownership of Java. Oracle now maintains the Java platform and its licensing.

mcq.q: Which language is the typed superset of JavaScript from Microsoft?
x: CoffeeScript is a language that compiles to JavaScript, but it is not a typed superset from Microsoft. It has a different, Ruby-inspired syntax.
Dart is a language from Google, used with Flutter. It is not a typed superset of JavaScript from Microsoft.
Kotlin is a language from JetBrains that runs on the JVM. It is not a JavaScript superset from Microsoft.
mcq.e: TypeScript, developed by Microsoft, is a typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript. It adds static type annotations to the language.

mcq.q: Which language is Google's preferred language for Android development since 2019?
x: Swift is Apple's language for iOS and macOS development, not Google's Android language. Google did not choose it for Android.
Dart is Google's language used with Flutter, not the preferred language for Android apps. It is for cross-platform UI.
Scala is a JVM language, not Google's preferred language for Android. It was not chosen for Android development.
mcq.e: Google announced Kotlin as its preferred language for Android development in 2019. Kotlin, created by JetBrains, works with Java code and libraries.

mcq.q: Which language is used for Apple's iOS development created by Apple in 2014?
x: Kotlin is a JetBrains language for the JVM and Android, not an Apple language. Apple did not create Kotlin.
Objective-C is Apple's older language, from the 1980s, and was replaced by Swift. It was not introduced in 2014.
Dart is a Google language used with Flutter. It is not Apple's language.
mcq.e: Swift was introduced by Apple in 2014 as a modern replacement for Objective-C for iOS and macOS apps. It is now open source.

mcq.q: Which language is used with the Flutter framework?
x: Go is a language from Google for systems and server software. It is not used to build Flutter apps.
Rust is a systems language focused on memory safety. It is not the language of Flutter.
Swift is Apple's language for iOS and macOS apps. It is not used with Flutter.
mcq.e: Flutter is Google's UI toolkit for building apps from one codebase, and its apps are written in Dart. Dart is a client-optimized language developed by Google.

mcq.q: Given int add(int a, int b) and double add(double a, double b) in one class, what does add(2, 3.0) return?
mcq.e: Only add(double,double) is applicable, because the int 2 widens to double but the double 3.0 cannot narrow to int. The compiler picks it at compile time, so the result is 5.0.
x: The int version is not applicable, because 3.0 cannot be narrowed to int, so the compiler does not choose it.
The call is not ambiguous, because only the double version is applicable. The compiler resolves it without error.
Overload resolution happens at compile time, so no runtime error arises. The call compiles and runs fine.

mcq.q: Which declaration is NOT a valid overload of int f(int x) in the same class?
mcq.e: Overloading needs a different parameter list; a different return type or parameter name does not count. double f(int y) has the same parameter list, so it clashes.
x: A different parameter count makes this a valid overload alongside f(int). The parameter list differs, so it is allowed.
A different parameter type, double instead of int, makes this a valid overload. Its parameter list differs.
A different parameter type, String, makes this a valid overload. The return type is not what matters; the parameter list differs.

mcq.q: Which pair of access modifiers both let a subclass in a different package access a member?
mcq.e: Default (package-private) blocks subclasses outside the package, and private blocks everything outside the class. Only public and protected reach such a subclass.
x: Default, or package-private, blocks subclasses outside the package. Protected lets such a subclass access the member, so this pair fails on default.
Both default and private block access from a subclass in a different package. Private blocks everything outside the class.
Default blocks a subclass in a different package, so this pair fails. Public alone would be enough.

mcq.q: In Java, class A has a constructor printing "A" and class B extends A has a constructor printing "B" with no explicit super call. What does new B() print?
mcq.e: The compiler inserts an implicit super() as the first statement of B's constructor, so the parent constructor runs first.
x: This would mean B's constructor runs first. Java runs the parent constructor before the subclass body.
This omits A's output. The implicit super() call always runs the parent constructor.
This omits B's output. B's constructor still runs after the parent constructor finishes.

mcq.q: class C { static int n = 0; int id; C(){ id = n++; } } After new C(); new C(); new C();, what are the third object's id and C.n?
mcq.e: n++ assigns the old value then increments: ids are 0, 1, 2, and the shared static n ends at 3. Pre-increment (++n) would have given ids 1, 2, 3.
x: This matches pre-increment, ++n, which gives ids 1, 2, 3. The code uses post-increment, so the third id is 2.
This gets the id right but undercounts n. Each object increments the shared counter once, so n ends at 3.
This matches neither result: the third id should be 2, and n should be 3 after three objects.

mcq.q: Given String s1 = "hi", s2 = "hi", s3 = new String("hi"), which expression is true?
mcq.e: Literals share one object in the string pool, so s1 == s2 is true. new String creates a separate heap object, so == against it is false even though equals() would be true.
x: s3 is a separate heap object from the literal s1, so the == comparison is false. Only equals would return true here.
s2 is a literal from the string pool, while s3 is a new heap object, so == is false.
Each new String expression creates a distinct object, so == compares two different references and is false.

mcq.q: Java: try { print "A"; return; } finally { print "F"; } What is printed?
mcq.e: The finally block runs even when the try block executes return, after A has been printed. So the output is A then F.
x: This omits the finally output. Finally still runs even when the try block executes a return.
This omits the A printed in the try block before the return. The try block runs before the finally.
This reverses the order. The finally block runs after the try block, so A comes first.

mcq.q: Java: try { print A; throw new RuntimeException(); } catch (Exception e) { print B; } finally { print C; } print D; What is the output?
mcq.e: The thrown exception is caught by catch (B), finally always runs (C), and since the exception was handled execution continues to D.
x: This skips B, but the exception is caught, so the catch block still runs and prints B.
This omits D. Since the exception was handled, execution continues after the try statement and prints D.
This puts D before the catch and finally. D runs only after the try, catch and finally blocks have completed.

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT an unchecked (runtime) exception in Java?
mcq.e: SQLException (like IOException) is a checked exception that must be handled or declared. The other three are runtime exceptions.
x: ArithmeticException extends RuntimeException, so it is unchecked. The question asks for the one that is not.
NullPointerException extends RuntimeException, so it is unchecked and need not be declared.
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException extends RuntimeException, so it is unchecked and need not be caught.

mcq.q: What is the combined size in bytes of one Java int, one long and one char?
mcq.e: int is 4, long is 8 and char is 2 bytes, so 4 + 8 + 2 = 14.
x: This drops the char size, so it counts only int plus long, which is 4 plus 8. A char takes 2 bytes in Java.
This assumes char takes 1 byte, as in C, which does not match Java's 2-byte char.
This assumes char takes 4 bytes. In Java, char is 2 bytes, a UTF-16 code unit.

mcq.q: Java: void change(int[] a){ a[0] = 9; a = new int[]{5}; } With int[] arr = {1}; change(arr); what is arr[0]?
mcq.e: The reference is copied (pass-by-value), so a[0] = 9 modifies the shared array. Reassigning the local copy of the reference does not affect arr.
x: This would be the value if the method did not change the shared array. The line a[0] = 9 does modify it.
This confuses the local reassignment a = new int[]{5} with changing arr. Reassigning the local copy does not affect arr.
The code is valid Java and compiles. An int array can be passed to an int[] parameter and modified.

mcq.q: Python: class D(B, C) where both B and C extend A. What is D's method resolution order?
mcq.e: C3 linearization keeps the order of the listed bases (B before C) and puts the shared parent A after both of them.
x: This puts A before C, which breaks C3 linearization. C must come before its base A.
This reverses the listed bases, putting C before B. Python keeps the order given in the class statement.
This puts A before its subclasses B and C. A class must come before its base classes.

mcq.q: Which pairing of language and diamond-problem solution is correct?
mcq.a: C++: virtual inheritance; Python: MRO (C3 linearization)
w: C++: MRO (C3 linearization); Python: virtual inheritance
Java: virtual inheritance; Python: interfaces only
C#: MRO (C3 linearization); C++: sealed classes
mcq.e: C++ uses virtual inheritance to keep a single shared base, while Python resolves the ambiguity with its MRO. Java and C# avoid it by disallowing multiple class inheritance.
x: This swaps the two. C++ uses virtual inheritance and Python uses MRO, so this pairing is wrong.
Java has no virtual inheritance because it does not allow multiple class inheritance. Python has no interfaces-only rule for this.
C# does not use C3 MRO for classes, and sealed classes prevent inheritance rather than resolve the diamond. This pairing is wrong.

mcq.q: Which statement is NOT true of a Java abstract class?
mcq.a: A class may extend several abstract classes at once
mcq.e: Java classes have single inheritance, so a class can extend only one abstract class (but may implement many interfaces). Abstract classes can still have constructors that subclasses call via super().
x: This is true: an abstract class can have concrete methods with bodies, so it is not the false statement.
This is true: abstract classes may declare abstract methods, so it is not the false statement.
This is true: abstract classes can declare constructors that subclasses call through super, so it is not the false statement.

mcq.q: Since Java 8, an interface may contain:
mcq.a: default and static methods with bodies
mcq.e: Java 8 added default and static methods to interfaces. Interfaces still have no constructors or instance state; their fields are implicitly public static final.
x: Interfaces cannot declare constructors, since they do not create objects. This is not something an interface may contain.
Interface fields are implicitly public static final constants, so they are not mutable instance fields.
Interface members are implicitly public, so protected members are not allowed in interfaces.

mcq.q: In Java, marking a method final means it:
mcq.a: cannot be overridden in a subclass
w: cannot be called from a subclass
mcq.e: final on a method blocks overriding only; overloads with different parameters are still allowed and subclasses can still call it.
x: Overloading is still allowed, since final only blocks overriding. A final method can be overloaded with different parameters.
A subclass can still call an inherited final method. Final blocks overriding, not calling.
final does not restrict access to instance fields. A final method can read and write them normally.

mcq.q: In C++, which call is resolved at run time through the vtable?
mcq.a: A virtual function called through a base-class pointer
w: A call to a static member function
mcq.e: Virtual functions use dynamic dispatch. Overloads, non-virtual and static member calls are bound at compile time.
x: Overloads are chosen at compile time by the parameter types, so no vtable lookup occurs.
Non-virtual calls are bound at compile time to the function named by the static type, so no vtable is used.
Static member functions are not tied to an object and are resolved at compile time, so no vtable is used.

mcq.q: A House and its Rooms, where the rooms are destroyed when the house is destroyed, is best described as:
mcq.e: Composition is the strongest has-a relationship: the parts cannot outlive the whole. Aggregation would let the parts exist independently.
x: Aggregation is a has-a relationship where parts can exist independently of the whole. The question says the rooms are destroyed with the house.
Association is a general link between classes with no lifetime dependency. It does not imply that parts die with the whole.
Realization is a UML relationship where a class implements an interface. It does not describe ownership of rooms.

mcq.q: Which Java version is NOT an LTS release?
mcq.e: Java 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25 are LTS releases. Java 16 (which finalized records) was a regular six-month release.
x: Java 11 is an LTS release, so it is not the non-LTS version the question asks for.
Java 17 is an LTS release, so it does not match the question.
Java 21 is an LTS release, so it does not match the question.

mcq.q: Which of these languages was released earliest?
mcq.e: Python came in 1991, Java and JavaScript in 1995, and C# in 2000.
x: Java came out in 1995, after Python's 1991 release. It is not the earliest.
JavaScript came out in 1995, also after Python's 1991 release. It is not the earliest.
C# came out in 2000, the latest of these languages. It is not the earliest.

mcq.q: Which statement about Java collections is correct?
mcq.a: ArrayList gives O(1) index access; LinkedList gives O(1) insertion at a known node
w: ArrayList gives O(1) middle insertion; LinkedList gives O(1) index access
Both give O(1) insertion at a known node without shifting
mcq.e: ArrayList is a dynamic array: fast random access but O(n) insertion in the middle because elements shift. LinkedList reverses that trade-off.
x: This swaps the trade-offs. ArrayList insertion in the middle needs shifting, so it is not O(1), and LinkedList has no O(1) index access.
Only ArrayList gives O(1) index access. LinkedList must walk its nodes, which is O(n).
ArrayList insertion requires shifting elements, so it is not O(1) without shifting. Only LinkedList has that property at a known node.

mcq.q: In Java, for int x = 5; Dog d = new Dog(); where are x and the Dog object stored?
mcq.a: x on the stack; the Dog object on the heap
w: x on the heap; the Dog object on the stack
mcq.e: Primitives local to a method and call frames live on the stack, while objects created with new live on the heap. The reference d itself is on the stack.
x: Places the object on the stack too. Only primitives and references live on the stack; the object created with new is always allocated on the heap.
Puts the local primitive x on the heap. Local variables of a method, including primitives, live in the stack frame, not on the heap.
Swaps both locations. The primitive x is a local and sits on the stack, while the Dog object created with new is on the heap.

mcq.q: Animal a = new Dog(); a.fetch(); where fetch() is defined only in Dog. What happens?
mcq.e: The compiler checks methods against the reference type Animal, which has no fetch(). A downcast ((Dog) a).fetch() would be needed.
x: Assumes the runtime type decides which method is visible. Method lookup uses the static type Animal, which has no fetch(), so the code will not compile.
A cast failure happens only when an explicit downcast is attempted on an incompatible object. No cast appears here, and the problem is caught earlier at compile time.
Happens when a method is called on a null reference. Here a is assigned a new Dog object, so it is not null, and the error is a compile-time one.

mcq.q: Java: void f(Animal x){print "A"} and void f(Dog x){print "D"} in one class, Dog extends Animal. After Animal a = new Dog(); f(a); what is printed?
mcq.e: Overloads are chosen at compile time from the declared (reference) type Animal, not the actual object. Only overriding uses run-time dispatch.
x: Would require run-time dispatch on the Dog object. Overloaded methods are picked by the declared type Animal, so f(Animal) is selected.
The code is legal Java. Overloading with parent and child parameter types is allowed, and the call f(a) resolves to f(Animal) without error.
Would mean f is never called or prints nothing. The call f(a) does execute and prints the letter for the selected overload, which is A.

mcq.q: A file Shop.java contains only: public class Store { }. What happens when compiling it?
mcq.a: Compile error: a public class must match the file name
w: It compiles to Store.class with a warning
It compiles and the file name is ignored
mcq.e: In Java a public class must be declared in a file with the same name, so Store must be in Store.java.
x: Assumes the file name determines the class name. The file contains class Store, and the public class rule rejects a mismatched file name before any class file is produced.
Treats the mismatch as a warning. In Java, a public class in a file with the wrong name is a hard compile error, not a warning.
Says the file name does not matter. Java requires a public class to be in a file with its exact name, so javac rejects this file.

mcq.q: A Java class declares only the constructor Dog(String name). What does new Dog() do?
mcq.a: Compile error: no default constructor is supplied
w: Creates a Dog with name null
Compiles; the compiler supplies a default constructor
Compiles but fails at run time
mcq.e: The compiler only provides a default constructor when the class defines no constructor at all.
x: Assumes a no-argument call quietly passes null for the String parameter. Java does not match Dog() to Dog(String), so no such object is created.
Assumes the implicit default constructor is always added. The compiler adds it only when no constructor is declared, and this class declares Dog(String).
Assumes the error is delayed until execution. The missing Dog() constructor is detected during compilation, so the program never runs.

mcq.q: In Python, an attribute named __x inside class Account is:
w: protected by a single leading underscore convention
mcq.e: Python has no true private members; double leading underscores trigger name mangling. A single underscore (_x) is only a convention.
x: Describes private access as in languages like Java. Python does not enforce it; the name is only mangled and can still be reached as _Account__x.
Confuses naming with storage scope. The double underscore prefix does not make an attribute class-level; static-ness is set by where it is declared.
Describes a single underscore, as in _x, not a double one. That is only a convention, while __x triggers name mangling.

mcq.q: Python: t = (1, [2]); t[1].append(3); print(t). What is the output?
mcq.e: A tuple is immutable but its elements are not: the list inside can still be mutated. Only reassigning t[1] would raise TypeError.
x: Assumes the append did not change the tuple. The tuple holds the same list object, and that list is mutated in place, so the inner list shows 3.
Would mean the list was unpacked into the tuple. append adds 3 to the inner list, so the tuple keeps two elements, not three.
Would occur only if t[1] were reassigned. Calling append on the inner list is allowed, so no error is raised.

mcq.q: Python: a = [1]; b = [1]; print(a == b, a is b). What is the output?
mcq.e: == compares values (equal lists) while is compares identity; a and b are two different list objects.
x: Claims a and b are the same object. Each [1] literal creates a new list, so is returns False even though == returns True.
Says the lists are not equal in value. Both contain 1, so == is True, and only the identity check is False.
Swaps the two results. == compares values and gives True, while is compares identity and gives False here.

mcq.q: In JavaScript, what do 5 == '5' and 5 === '5' evaluate to, in that order?
mcq.e: == coerces types so the string becomes the number 5; === is strict equality and requires the same type.
x: Swaps the results of both comparisons. == coerces '5' to 5 and gives true, while === checks types and gives false.
Assumes === also coerces types. Strict equality compares types first, so a number and a string are never strictly equal.
Assumes == does not coerce the string. Loose equality converts '5' to the number 5, so the result is true.
